title: Al-Bayyinah: the clear proof
hook: the People of the Book and others awaited a clear sign (Surah 98)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Az-Zalzalah again, the earth that tells what was done on it. Your line was the ground remembers. Did you walk a little more gently, and where? Day one hundred seventy-eight.

One day, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ went to a companion named Ubayy ibn Ka'b, a man known for his recitation, and said something strange. Allah has commanded me to recite to you: those who disbelieve, the opening of Surah al-Bayyinah. Ubayy asked: did He name me? The Prophet said: yes. And Ubayy wept. It's in Sahih al-Bukhari. A man hears that his own name was spoken by the Lord of the worlds, and he cries. Of all the surahs, this was the one chosen for that moment. Today: Al-Bayyinah, the clear proof.
screen: `RECITE IT TO UBAYY.` → `DID HE NAME ME?` → `AND UBAYY WEPT.`

segments.voice: Bayyinah means a clear proof, evidence you can see, something that makes a matter plain. The root is b-y-n, to be distinct, to stand out clearly, the same root as bayan, a clear statement. The surah opens by describing people waiting. Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book, a phrase commentators apply to Jews and Christians, and among the polytheists, the surah says, would not let go of their ways until the clear proof came to them. Then it names that proof: a messenger from Allah, reciting purified pages, containing upright writings. For Muslims, that's the Prophet and the Qur'an he recited. There's a quiet line after that. The surah notes that the People of the Book did not divide until after the clear proof had come to them. Commentators read it as a pattern the Qur'an describes more than once: clarity itself can become the place people disagree. A sign doesn't end argument; sometimes it starts it. The surah then describes, in its closing verses, two kinds of people and their ends, and speaks of those who believe and do good as the best of creation, well pleased with Allah and He with them. Tomorrow we'll hear the verse in the middle, about what was actually asked of everyone. Today, just the word. A clear proof is something that makes things plain enough to choose. The Qur'an presents itself that way: not as a riddle, but as bayyinah, something clear. What people do with clarity is another matter.
screen: `BAYYINAH — EVIDENCE YOU CAN SEE.` · `PEOPLE WAITING FOR A SIGN.` · `A MESSENGER, PURIFIED PAGES.` · `CLARITY CAN BECOME A DISPUTE.` · then, large: `CLEAR PROOF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one clear verse. After this lesson, find one short verse of the Qur'an, from any translation you have, or from a surah you've met here, like by time, or he is one. Read it once, slowly. For now, sit and think of something in your life that is actually clear, that you already know is right, and that you've been putting off anyway. Just let it be plain. The bell holds the time.
Al-Bayyinah. The clear proof, evidence that makes a matter plain; the name of Surah ninety-eight. Today's word.
Your line: clear proof. Today, take one thing you already know clearly is right, and do it, instead of waiting for a bigger sign. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Bayyinah in the prayers, and the hadith of the Prophet reciting it to Ubayy ibn Ka'b is often told as a sign of honor for those who learn and recite the Qur'an.

original.note: Arabic: the clear proof, from b-y-n, to be distinct and plain.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah about proof, like an argument.
what it means: the clear evidence people awaited, which Muslims understand as the Prophet and the Qur'an he recited.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 4959 (Ubayy); 98:4 on division after the clear proof; commentators differ on whether it is Meccan or Medinan.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4959 (the Prophet recites it to Ubayy)

notes: All of Surah 98 is paraphrased here; Pickthall not quoted because the writer wasn't certain of the exact wording of 98:1–4.

The script identifies 'People of the Book' as the Jews and Christians of Arabia, following the standard reading, and describes 98:4 as a pattern of division without judging any group. A Keeper should check the tone of this passage carefully, since the surah's closing verses (98:6) speak of the fate of those who disbelieve; the script mentions 'two kinds of people and their ends' without detail.

Reviewer edit: the teach now paraphrases 98:1 as 'those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists', matching the verse's qualifier, instead of implying all Jews and Christians of Arabia; 'polytheists of Mecca' narrowed to 'polytheists'. Keeper please check.
'Best of creation' paraphrases 98:7; 'well pleased with Allah and He with them' paraphrases 98:8.
Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the uncited superlative 'one of the best reciters in Medina' (now 'known for his recitation'); the hook no longer uses 'Imagine'.
